issues.title: Config file discovery doesn't work as intended
issues.body:
As it stated in the [documentation](https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools#configuration), pip-tools look for the configuration file “in the same directory as your requirements input files”. However, due to the way click works, it's not true:

1. `--config` (and `--no-config`) is declared as eager: https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/blob/7.4.1/piptools/scripts/options.py#L317-L333
2. `--config`'s callback `override_defaults_from_config_file` tries to get the `src_files` param value to compute the config path relative to the source files: https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/blob/7.4.1/piptools/utils.py#L543
3. But since callbacks of eager options are called before other options are processed, `src_files` is always empty. From the [click documentation](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/8.1.x/advanced/#callback-evaluation-order): “All eager parameters are evaluated before all non-eager parameters, but again in the order as they were provided on the command line by the user.” 
4. `select_config_file` falls back to the current working dir as a config file location: https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/blob/7.4.1/piptools/utils.py#L627-L630

#### Environment Versions

1. Linux
1. Python version: `Python 3.12.3`
1. pip version: `pip 24.0`
1. pip-tools version: `pip-compile, version 7.4.1`

#### Steps to replicate

1. Create the requirements directory `requirements/` with `requirements.in`.
1. Create the configuration file `.pip-tools.toml` or `pyproject.toml` with `generate-hashes = true`.
1. Run `pip compile requirements/requirements.in`. 

#### Expected result

 `requirements/requirements.txt` contains hashes.

#### Actual result

 `requirements/requirements.txt` has no hashes; the configuration file is ignored.

issues.title: pip-compile should accept special files (pipes, fifo, pty, sockets, ...) as output files
issues.body:
When running `pip-compile -o /dev/stdout`, the command blocks indefinitely. It shouldn't and should write the requirement file in the given file, even if it's not a bare file. 

Please note that `pip-compile | <other program>` doesn't work either (the other program doesn't receive anything).

Please also note that `stderr` is cluttered by some eventual warnings not parseable by pip and is so not usable as a viable content source.

#### Environment Versions

1. > Linux VirtualBox 5.4.0-165-generic # 182-Ubuntu SMP Mon Oct 2 19:43:28 UTC 2023 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
1. > Python version: Python 3.8.10
1. > pip version: pip 23.3.1
1. > pip-tools version: pip-compile, version 7.3.0

#### Steps to replicate

1. `git clone <your favourite "using setup.py" project> && cd in`
2. `pip-compile setup.py -o /dev/stdout`
3. nothing happens

#### Expected result

output on stdout (**not stderr**)
warnings (if any) on stderr

#### Actual result
\<nothing and process blocked>


#### Steps to replicate (advanced)
TTY 1 :
1. `mkfifo /tmp/mylovelyfifo`
2. `cat /tmp/mylovelyfifo`

TTY 2 :
1. `git clone <your favourite "using setup.py" project> && cd in`
2. `pip-compile setup.py -o /tmp/mylovelyfifo`

#### Expected result

output on TTY 1
warnings (if any) on TTY 2

#### Actual result
\<nothing and process blocked>

comments.author: manuco
comments.body:
The main problem is that `pip compile` try to **read** the **output file** in order to find previous requirement and update it. `pip compile` should ensure that previous requirements is only read from a **real file** (with [stat.S_ISREG(mode)](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stat.html)), but should not trust that reading from this file won't block.

For example, setting `/dev/stdout` as an output file will make `pip compile` try to read this file. And it won't generate any error because `/dev/stdout` as a link to your terminal (`/dev/pts/*n*`) is also readable (since `/dev/pts/*n*` is also stdin and stderr). But it won't give any data until you type on your keyboard (which is not what's expected).

issues.title: support per-requirement options
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

`pip` supports [per-requirement options](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/reference/requirements-file-format/#per-requirement-options), e.g. `--config-settings`

I'm forced to use per-requirement `--config-settings`, because there are [cases where pip intentionally does not honor the command-line `--config-settings`](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/reference/build-system/pyproject-toml/#backend-configuration).

> Configuration settings provided via --config-settings command line options (or the equivalent environment variables or configuration file entries) are passed to the build of requirements explicitly provided as pip command line arguments. They are not passed to the build of dependencies, or to the build of requirements provided in requirement files.

But `pip-compile` does not seem to propagate per-requirement options.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

I'd like pip-compile to propagate per-requirement options from `.in` to `.txt`

```
$ echo 'scipy==1.10.1; --config-settings="setup-args=-Dblas=blas"' > r.in

$ pip-compile -r r.in
numpy==1.24.4
    # via scipy
scipy==1.10.1; --config-settings="setup-args=-Dblas=blas"
    # via -r r2.in
```

#### Alternative Solutions

Command line `pip --config-settings` doesn't work, because I'm passing a requirements file to `pip wheel`, and pip intentionally doesn't propagate the settings.

My current workaround is to build the affected packages separately, avoiding use of a requirements file.  But it's not good for my use case, which is to build all the transitive dependencies for an application (targeting an alternative python implementation).  `pip wheel -r ...` is best suited for this.

issues.title: pre-commit hook for pip-sync
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

With the pre-commit hook for pip-compile (https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/974), I am confident that any changes that I do in my development environment will be pinned. I would like to have the same for pip-sync so that nobody's development environment gets outdated.

In a project, it might be that one of the collaborators have modified the dependencies and pushed their new pip-compiled requirements.txt. As I get their changes via a `git pull`, I want to be sure that we (everyone) keep sharing the same dependencies. As far as I see with the current pip-tools workflow, pip-sync has to be run manually. That means, I have to be informed by the collaborator or check the pulled/merged commits to see if I need to run pip-sync. This could lead to some issues, could we automate pip-sync so that we avoid those?

If it gets implemented, the new hook combined with the existing pip-compile hook would allow a mostly automated dependency management.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

I am no expert at pre-commit, but I think it can be used for developing a new hook similar to that of pip-compile(https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/pull/976). I believe one can use the [post-merge](https://pre-commit.com/#post-merge) `stage` for this hook.

.pre-commit-hooks.yaml for the new hook would something like the following:

```yaml
- id: pip-sync
  name: pip-sync
  description: Automatically sync requirements.
  entry: pip-sync
  language: python
  files: ^requirements\.(in|txt)$
  args: [--ask]
  
```

#### Alternative Solutions

Simply printing a message that the environment needs to modified could be a better default option as it is not intrusive (https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/1076). issues.title: Upgrading an extra package leaks it into the install_requires
issues.body:
I think I've hit an edge case with pip-tools and setuptools. I couldn't find a similar open issue.

When selectively upgrading packages for the base dependencies (`install_requires`), requesting an upgrade for a package that's declared in the optional dependencies (`extras_require`) causes it to leak into the generated `requirements.txt` file, **even if the `--extra` was *not* selected**.

#### Environment Versions

1. Pop!_OS 22.04 LTS
1. Python 3.11.3
1. pip 23.1.2
1. pip-compile, version 6.13.0

#### Steps to replicate

1. create `setup.py`
```
echo 'from setuptools import setup

setup(
    install_requires=["requests"],
    extras_require={"dev": ["hodor"]},
)' > setup.py
```

2. prepare environment
```
virtualenv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install pip-tools
# generate initial requirements.txt
.venv/bin/pip-compile --resolver backtracking
```

3. upgrade an optional dependency and a dependency that's not declared anywhere
```
.venv/bin/pip-compile --resolver backtracking -P hodor -P numpy -o broken-requirements.txt
```

#### Expected result

```
certifi==2023.5.7
    # via requests
charset-normalizer==3.1.0
    # via requests
idna==3.4
    # via requests
requests==2.31.0
    # via UNKNOWN (setup.py)
urllib3==2.0.2
    # via requests
```

#### Actual result

```
certifi==2023.5.7
    # via requests
charset-normalizer==3.1.0
    # via requests
hodor==1!0  #  <------------------- shouldn't be here
idna==3.4
    # via requests
requests==2.31.0
    # via UNKNOWN (setup.py)
urllib3==2.0.2
    # via requests
```

pip-tools correctly ignores the `numpy` package, as it is not declared anywhere, but seems to be tricked by `hodor`, which is an extra dependency from the `dev` group. It is also missing the comment that tells why the dependency was included.

I've checked with a plain setup.py and a combination of setup.py and setup.cfg and both trigger this behavior.  Does not seem related to the choice of resolver either. Using a `requirements-dev.in` that references a `requirements.in` seems to work as expected.

### Motivation

Currently, `pip-compile` by default will emit any index URLs used.

For open source users, likely this will be empty (no index URL).  Regardless of the default being `--no-emit-index-url` or not, these users will not be affected, as just PyPI is used.

For non-open source users, this may not be empty.  For these users, forgetting to include `--no-emit-index-url` represents a security risk, because if this opt-in arg is forgotten, a company secret will be leaked.

This actually happened to me tonight when I accidentally leaked my company's internal package manager's index URL.  Luckily, I realized it within 15 minutes, and refreshed my token.  Now I am getting an email from GitGuardian saying their service detected a string secret was leaked.

For all of my company's `pip-compile` use cases, we append `--no-emit-index-url`.  Thus for engineers at my company, a useful default would be `--no-emit-index-url`.

### Request

I think the default of `pip-compile` should be secure (and not bias towards leaking secrets).

This entails:
1. Making `--no-emit-index-url` the new default
2. Adding `--emit-index-url` or `--enable-emit-index-url` as an opt-in flag

issues.title: pip-compile with --index-url fails to handle sdists
issues.body:
I'm trying to use pip-tools in an environment where we have access to a caching proxy (Artifactory) of pypi.org but no direct access to pypi.org.

In most situations, I'm able to run `pip-compile` in a virtualenv where I've set `index-url` in `pip.conf`, and everything works. However, I'm now trying to get dependabot working, and dependabot invokes `pip-compile` and passes `--index-url`, but doesn't set `index-url` for `pip` in any way (environment variables or `pip.conf`). 

In this environment (and in my local environment I can reproduce it, if I move `pip.conf` aside), when `pip-compile` encounters a package that only has an sdist and not a wheel (e.g. defopt), it tries to run `python setup.py egg_info` on the sdist, and that runs `python3 -m pip --disable-pip-version-check wheel --no-deps -w /tmp/something --quiet setuptools_scm>=3.3`, which fails after trying to connect to `pypi.org` and getting blocked at our firewall.

I think, probably, `pip-compile --index-url` should change how it invokes `python setup.py egg_info` such that that call is also aware of the index url. One simple way would be to set `PIP_INDEX_URL`, but you all probably could get more clever about pip than I can.

#### Environment Versions

1. OS Type: Linux (Debian 10)
1. Python version: `$ python -V` 3.11.1
1. pip version: `$ pip --version` 23.0.1
1. pip-tools version: `$ pip-compile --version` 6.12.3

#### Steps to replicate

1. Create a `requirements.in` containing one line, `defopt`
2. Block access to pypi.org, use some alternative pypi mirror (devpi would be fine)
3. Run `pip-compile -vv --index-url=https://pypi.internal/simple --resolver backtracking requirements.in`

#### Expected result

It should result in a `requirements.txt` file.

#### Actual result

The command fails, with some stacktraces ending in `pip._internal.exceptions.MetadataGenerationFailed: metadata generation failed`

issues.title: Error: input and output filenames must not be matched
issues.body:
Error: input and output filenames must not be matched

#### Environment Versions

1. OS Type: Windows 11
2. Python version: 3.9.17
3. pip version: 23.0.1
4. pip-tools version: 6.12.2

#### Steps to replicate

Using command as per comments in and existing compiled requirements.txt after adding a new dependency in file.

```
#
# This file is autogenerated by pip-compile with Python 3.9
# by the following command:
#
#    pip-compile --annotation-style=line ./bin/app/requirements.txt
#
click==8.1.3              # via flask
flask==2.2.2              # via flask-failsafe
flask-failsafe==0.2       # via -r ./bin/app/requirements.txt
importlib-metadata==6.0.0  # via flask
itsdangerous==2.1.2       # via flask
jinja2==3.1.2             # via flask
markupsafe==2.1.2         # via jinja2, werkzeug
werkzeug==2.2.2           # via flask
zipp==3.11.0              # via importlib-metadata
gunicorn # New dependecy
```

Executed

`pip-compile --annotation-style=line ./bin/app/requirements.txt`

#### Expected result

File recompiled with new dependency fixed and added dependencies.

#### Actual result

`Error: input and output filenames must not be matched`

#### Notes

This appears to be caused by changes in this PR https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/pull/1787 "Raise error if input and output filenames are matched"

I can understand thinking behind the change but there is little risk of updating file in place when using version control, it means that to add a new dependency I have to copy the file first and add an --output-file parameter, then delete the input file, or manage two files in the repository going forward.

It is also at odds with the deriving of output file name from input as specified as a option in help:

```
  -o, --output-file FILENAME      Output file name. Required if more than one
                                  input file is given. Will be derived from
                                  input file otherwise.
```

It breaks backwards compatibility withe the command list in comments in the output file.

Suggestion either remove this check or add a flag such as `--allow-overwrite` to suppress the check.

comments.author: AndydeCleyre
comments.body:
The idea of the tool is to keep a `requirements.in` file with your explicit, top level dependencies, versioned as loosely as possible, then generate a fully version locked, deep dependency tree/list as `requirements.txt`.

If you then remove the `.in` file and compile using the locked `.txt` as a source, you lose the information of which dependencies are explicit/top level, and you lose the possibility of the versions getting updated, because they're already locked in exactly.

It is very unlikely that is any user's intent.

The tool has worked fine using a single file before this change and if the "idea of this tool" is not to ever use a single file why does the help for `--output-file` specify `Required if more than one input file is given.  Will be derived from input file otherwise`?

That's two files, not a single file. The input file is the `.in`, and the output file is the `.txt`.

issues.title: Generate both the requirements file and the corresponding contraints file in one command
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Our application uses two sets of requirements:

* requirements.in
* requirements-dev.in

Previously, we would add `-c requirements.txt` at the top of our `requirements-dev.in` to ensure that compatible packages get installed, as described in the "Workflow for layered requirements" section of pip-tools' README.

Since pip changed how `-c` works by restricting what's allowed in "constraints files" (https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/user_guide/#constraints-files), we can no longer put `-c requirements.txt` at the top of our `requirements-dev.in`.

This is because our `requirements.txt` contains entries that are not allowed to be in a constraints file, including extras and `file:` (ie. vendored) dependencies.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

One solution would be to have a command line option in pip-tools to generate a valid constraints file in addition to the requirements file. Something like this:

```
pip-compile --resolver=backtracking requirements.in -o requirements.txt --output-as-constraint-file requirements-as-constraints.txt
```

We would then be able to add `-c requirements-as-constraints.txt`  to the top of our `requirements-dev.in` and have a similar workflow as before. Having both the requirements.txt and requirements-as-constraints.txt files generated in one command would also ensure that they are in sync.

#### Alternative Solutions

I couldn't find a simple workflow for what we're trying to do . pip-tools has `--strip-extras` but this doesn't help for `file:` dependencies, and it also would require an extra command to generate a constraints file.

Our current approach, which is unideal, is to just copy and paste problematic entries from the requirements.in to the requirement-dev.in.

#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

I saw that if I run `pip-compile -i <url> --resolver=backtracking --verbose requirements.in`, then dependencies are always downloaded from the provided index url. In contrast, if I run the same command without `-i` flag, then cached version of packages may be used, which results in much fast compiling time.

Pip itself is able to cache packages from such indexes. If I run `pip install -i <url> package==1.2.3`, then the distributed binary will end up in cache. Next time I invoke the same command, there will be no download.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

I would like pip-compile to cache dependency information from third party indices similar to how it does it for PyPI.

Probably the main benefit will be for people who develop non-public packages, that are uploaded to private indices.
